title: Knowledge Check 2: Lessons 9-16
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 9-16 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Two providers both support function calling. Why can the same tool-calling code fail after a switch from one to the other?
options: Each provider uses its own request and response shape.
Only one of them runs the tool on the provider's servers.
Function calling needs the model retrained for each provider.
Tool definitions must be rewritten in a different language.
questions.explanation: Providers expose the same capability through different request and response shapes, so client code written for one dialect is not portable to another without an adapter.

questions.question: A provider sometimes returns tool arguments as a JSON string and sometimes as an already-parsed object. How should a portable client handle this?
options: Send the raw provider response straight to the downstream tool
Require every provider to return arguments as a JSON string
Parse each provider's response into one common internal result
Reorder the tool definitions until the response shapes match
questions.explanation: Responses differ by provider, so a per-provider parser that maps each shape to one internal result keeps the rest of the agent identical across providers.

questions.question: A local model accepts OpenAI-style tool calls but returns JSON that fails to parse. What does this demonstrate?
options: The model needs a larger context window to emit valid JSON
Compatible wire format does not guarantee reliable calls
Local models cannot support tool calling in any configuration
The schema must be rewritten in the provider's native dialect
questions.explanation: A provider can speak a compatible wire format yet still return malformed or incomplete arguments, so parsed arguments must be validated before a tool runs.

questions.question: Why are documents split into chunks before they are embedded?
options: So the model can generate longer answers from each one
So each chunk fits the model limit and stands alone
So the same text never appears in more than one chunk
So chunk order is preserved when the index is rebuilt
questions.explanation: Embedding models have limited input length and a chunk must carry enough meaning to be found, so documents are split into self-contained pieces.

questions.question: Why must a query be embedded with the same model that embedded the stored documents?
options: A different model would refuse to process the query at all
The stored vectors must be reordered for each new model
Only models trained on the same corpus can answer a query
Vectors from different models are not comparable
questions.explanation: An index and a query land in the same vector space only when produced by the same model, so any other model makes the comparison meaningless.

questions.question: A RAG system gives fluent, well-cited answers that are wrong or outdated. Where should you invest first?
options: The knowledge source and the retrieval step
A larger and more capable base model
A longer prompt with more detailed instructions
A faster response time for each generated answer
questions.explanation: Retrieval quality depends on the knowledge source and the retrieval step far more than on the model, so the data pipeline is the highest-leverage fix.

questions.question: An embedding model is trained to place which pieces of text near each other in vector space?
options: Text that mentions the same words
Text that comes from the same author
Text that carries a similar meaning
Text of roughly the same length
questions.explanation: Embeddings map text by meaning, so passages with similar sense land close together even when they share no words.

questions.question: Why is cosine similarity the standard way to compare two embeddings?
options: It compares the direction of the vectors, not their length
It returns the exact number of shared words between the inputs
It normalizes both vectors to the same number of dimensions
It measures the raw distance between the two points in space
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity compares the angle between the vectors, so it captures direction of meaning rather than magnitude.

questions.question: A vector search misses a query built around a rare product code. What is the underlying reason?
options: The index was built with too few dimensions for the code
Rare or unseen exact terms embed poorly and match as noise
The query returned too many results to rank the code highly
The stored chunk was filtered out by its metadata first
questions.explanation: General embedding models handle rare terms and exact identifiers poorly, which is why an exact-term query needs a keyword path as well.

questions.question: Why does a vector database use approximate nearest neighbor search instead of checking every vector?
options: Exact search is undefined for high-dimensional vectors
Approximate search returns a more accurate result
Exact search scales linearly and becomes too slow
Approximate search stores each vector in fewer bytes
questions.explanation: Checking every vector scales linearly with the corpus, so fast search accepts a small accuracy tradeoff to keep queries sublinear.

questions.question: A team already runs PostgreSQL and needs vector search for a moderate corpus. What is the recommended starting point?
options: Add pgvector and query beside relational data
Stand up a dedicated distributed vector cluster
Keep all the vectors in application memory
Wait until the corpus reaches billions of vectors
questions.explanation: Starting with the least extra infrastructure that proves the idea is the rule, and an existing Postgres deployment makes pgvector the lowest-friction choice.

questions.question: A team gets poor retrieval results and considers moving to a larger vector database. What influences answer quality more?
options: The number of server nodes dedicated to the search cluster
The specific index algorithm selected by the database
The average query latency the database can sustain
The chunking and embedding choices behind the index
questions.explanation: The store sets how fast near-neighbors are found, not whether the right chunks are findable, which is decided by the chunking and embedding upstream.

questions.question: A retriever finds the right chunk but ranks it fortieth. Which lever fixes that?
options: Raising the number of chunks passed to the model
Re-embedding the corpus with a larger model
Reranking the shortlist with a cross-encoder
Adding metadata filters to the query
questions.explanation: A reranker rescores a shortlist with full attention over query and document, lifting the right chunk to the top among results already found.

questions.question: A query fails because an exact part number never appears in the results. Which lever fixes it?
options: Reranking the candidates with a cross-encoder
Hybrid search that adds a keyword path
A larger top-k cutoff on the vector search
A metadata filter on document status
questions.explanation: Exact identifiers are exactly what dense vectors miss, so pairing vector similarity with keyword matching is what surfaces them.

questions.question: Before any ranking, what does a metadata filter on retrieved chunks decide?
options: Which chunks are eligible to be returned
How many chunks the model is allowed to see
The order the chunks are passed to the model
How similar each chunk is to the query
questions.explanation: Metadata filtering sets eligibility, scope, and access before ranking, so the model never sees a chunk the user cannot see.

questions.question: In an agent's memory design, what does the context window represent?
options: Long-term storage that survives across sessions
A log of every past conversation
A record of the agent's learned skills
Working memory, bounded by token limits
questions.explanation: The context window is the agent's working memory: fast and always present, but strictly bounded by token limits.

questions.question: What distinguishes episodic memory from semantic memory?
options: Episodic holds facts, semantic holds events
Episodic records events, semantic holds facts
Episodic persists across sessions, semantic does not
Episodic is written by users, semantic by the model
questions.explanation: Episodic memory stores time-indexed experiences of what happened, while semantic memory stores general facts that hold across contexts.

questions.question: An agent stores every message forever and surfaces a fact that was true last month but is not anymore. What is the flaw?
options: It never consolidates or demotes outdated facts
It sends too little context to the model each turn
It keeps the context window smaller than the store
It mixes episodic and semantic memory in one table
questions.explanation: An unbounded store that is never consolidated keeps stale facts at the same standing as current ones, so the agent confidently repeats what is no longer true.

questions.question: Context rot describes which behavior?
options: Recall drops as the context grows longer
Recall improves as more examples are added
Answers get shorter as the window fills
Cost falls as the context is trimmed
questions.explanation: As the window fills with tokens, the model's ability to recall information from its context degrades, a slide known as context rot.

questions.question: What does trimming (pruning) do, as opposed to summarization?
options: It rewrites old content into a shorter paraphrase
It removes content rather than rewriting it
It moves old content into a separate store
It increases the window so nothing is lost
questions.explanation: Trimming deletes content that no longer earns its keep, with no rewriting, which makes it cheaper and less distorting than a summary.

questions.question: What is the recommended strategy for keeping a long-running agent coherent?
options: Summarize every turn to keep the window small
Buy a larger window so nothing needs removal
Trim routinely and summarize only rarely
Keep every observation so nothing is lost
questions.explanation: Cheap deletion handles the steady accumulation while the expensive summary is reserved for runs that genuinely threaten the window.

questions.question: A language model is stateless. What does that mean for a multi-turn conversation?
options: The model retains a short memory of the prior turn
Multi-turn behavior must be built by the application
The model refuses to answer without a prior message
The provider stores the conversation on the model's behalf
questions.explanation: Each model call is standalone, so the application layer must store the state and reattach the relevant slice of it to every new call.

questions.question: In a resumable agent, what is the difference between the session and the state?
options: The session is the identity; the state is its content
The session is stored on disk; the state lives in the window
The session is per user; the state is per model
The session is temporary; the state is deleted each turn
questions.explanation: The session is the identity that ties turns together, while the state is everything the session must remember to keep behaving coherently.

questions.question: An agent runs in containers that restart, yet it resumes conversations correctly. What must it use?
options: An in-memory saver for the conversation thread
A durable store keyed by a thread identifier
A larger context window to hold prior turns
A state object that stores full document text
questions.explanation: Resuming after a process restart requires state persisted outside memory, kept under a stable identifier so the same conversation can be reloaded.
